page: Microsoft Azure FX16-8mds_v2 is a constrained-vCPU virtual machine hosted on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It runs on a dedicated x86_64 Intel Xeon 8573C processor with 4 physical cores and 8 vCPUs operating at a 4.2 GHz base frequency. The architecture features 260 MB of L3 cache and supports specialized instruction sets including AVX-512, Intel AMX tile, and AMX int8 extensions. System memory is provisioned at 336.0 GB, resulting in an allocation of 42.0 GB per vCPU. The instance incorporates 944 GB of direct-attached NVMe SSD storage. It contains zero GPUs and does not include complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark evaluations reveal strong single-core performance driven by the high clock frequency. The server achieved a single-core Geekbench score of 2165.0 and completed single-threaded gzip compression at 34.31 GB/sec, placing both results in the upper quartile. Text processing reached 2931.0 in Geekbench, placing it in the top decile. In multi-threaded testing, performance is constrained by the 8 vCPU limit, producing median-tier results of 7546.0 in multi-core Geekbench and 8882.55 in multi-core stress-ng. Memory bandwidth reached 44.97 GB/sec for uncached 256 MB reads and 32.17 GB/sec for writes. For machine learning inference, small 135M model text generation reached 315.18 tokens per second, though medium 7B model generation fell to the lower quartile at 8.54 tokens per second.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the constrained core configuration optimizes per-core software licensing expenditures while maintaining access to large system memory and high clock speeds. The inclusion of 944 GB of fast NVMe local storage reduces reliance on external block devices for temporary data. The principal architectural tradeoff is limited horizontal parallelism, as total multi-core throughput is constrained by the 8 vCPU boundary despite the massive memory footprint.

The FX16-8mds_v2 is suitable for per-core licensed relational database engines, high-capacity in-memory data stores such as Redis, electronic design automation (EDA), batch text analysis, and data engineering workloads requiring high clock speeds and substantial RAM per thread.
